title: Fifty-two tassels
told: a traditional story of Guru Hargobind

hook.say: before the story, a question. when something good comes your way, who do you think of first?
options: then you’ll like this guru. listen.
that’s honest. most of us do. this guru didn’t. listen.
then you’ll understand this guru. listen.

steps.line: The sixth Guru, Guru Hargobind, was held prisoner in the great fort of Gwalior by the Mughal emperor, Jahangir.
steps.label: a traditional story

steps.line: Also held there were fifty-two Hindu princes. Over time, the Guru became their friend.
At last the emperor ordered the Guru set free. But the Guru said: I won’t leave without them.

steps.q: The fifty-two were Hindu princes; the Guru was a Sikh. Why does that detail matter to Sikhs?
o: He freed people not of his faith
The princes had paid for his release
It won him the princes’ armies
steps.why: He wouldn’t walk out free while others stayed captive, whoever they were. Freedom for everyone, not just his own.

steps.q: The Guru won’t leave without the fifty-two. What do you think the emperor says?
o: Fine, free them all, in your honor
Then stay, all of you, together
Only those who can hold your robe
steps.why: A trap dressed as a favor: as many as could hold on to the Guru’s robe could leave with him. He expected only a few.

steps.line: The emperor was sure only a few could hold on. So the Guru had a robe made with fifty-two tassels.
He walked out of the gate, and behind him walked all fifty-two princes, each holding a tassel. Sikhs remember him as Bandi Chhor, the one who sets captives free.
Tradition says he reached Amritsar at Diwali, and the city lit lamps. Sikhs still light up the Golden Temple for Bandi Chhor Divas.
steps.label: today

steps.pre: Guru Hargobind wore two swords: piri for the spirit, and miri for
steps.why: Miri and piri: a Sikh looks after both, the spirit and the world. He built the Akal Takht facing the Harmandir Sahib for the same reason.

steps.q: Years before, under the same emperor, the Guru’s father, Guru Arjan, died in custody. What does that add?
o: The emperor wanted to make peace
The Guru had every reason to run
The princes were Guru Arjan’s friends
steps.why: Guru Arjan was put to death in 1606 under Jahangir. His son, held by the same emperor, still wouldn’t walk out alone.

say: remember guru nanak’s twenty rupees, spent feeding hungry people? he called it sacha sauda, the true bargain. here it is again, more than a century later, in a fort.
sikhs believe a deal that’s only good for you isn’t a true one. vand chhakna means sharing what you have, even your freedom. the guru’s good news was only good once everyone could hold on.

steps.q: From the story, how is the robe like Guru Nanak’s twenty rupees?
o: Both were gifts from an emperor
Both were ways to win followers
Both were spent on other people
steps.why: Twenty rupees fed the hungry. Fifty-two tassels freed the captives. The true bargain, twice.

today.say: today, when something good comes your way, a ticket, a discount, a lucky break, find one way to let someone else hold on to it too. that’s vand chhakna.
options: then you’re a tassel-maker. i love that.
then share what you have: an hour, a meal, a ride.

tomorrow.line: the guru asks his sons to carry a dripping bundle. they say no. someone else says yes.

card.from: a traditional story of Guru Hargobind
card.keepWhy: Freedom is only true when others can hold on.
sources: Sikh tradition of Guru Hargobind’s imprisonment at Gwalior Fort under Jahangir and his release with fifty-two rajas holding his robe
Bandi Chhor Divas, kept at Diwali, with the illumination of the Harmandir Sahib
check: Historians debate the length and dates of the Gwalior imprisonment (often c. 1617-1619) and whether fifty-two is literal; story labeled tradition.
Some tellings credit Mian Mir with pleading for the release; I left it out.
Reaching Amritsar at Diwali is tradition. The day-26 script topic was sacha sauda; that story was told in week one, so this lesson carries the same teaching through Bandi Chhor.
